summary: Describes using a Service Function Forwarder label, similar to a pseudowire or VPN label, to mark that a Network Service Header sits between an MPLS label stack and the original packet. This lets SFC packets cross an MPLS network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to wrap packets carrying service instructions inside an MPLS envelope, with a special label that says 'instructions inside'.

questions: mpls transport for service function chaining
how do you carry nsh in mpls
how does mpls transport service function chaining
subtitle: Transporting Service Function Chaining packets through MPLS networks using a label.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining packets with Network Service Headers need a way to cross MPLS networks so that service functions in different network domains can cooperate.
tldr.mechanism: An MPLS label called the SFF Label (Service Function Forwarder label) is placed at the bottom of the label stack to indicate that an NSH sits between the label stack and the original packet.
tldr.outcome: This allows SFC packets to be forwarded between Service Function Forwarders across MPLS transport networks using standard MPLS procedures without requiring any new protocol extensions.

facts.label: NSH placement
facts.value: Between MPLS label stack and original packet

today: RFC 8596 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes a method for using existing MPLS procedures to carry SFC NSH packets, without requiring changes to the MPLS protocol itself.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC describes how to use the MPLS label stack to transport packets that are already carrying a Network Service Header (NSH). The NSH is part of Service Function Chaining (SFC), which lets network operators insert specialized processing steps (service functions) into the path a packet takes through the network.

Rather than defining a new protocol, this document shows how to apply existing, well-established MPLS procedures. The key mechanism is an SFF Label (Service Function Forwarder label) that sits at the bottom of an MPLS label stack and tells the receiving node that an NSH follows.

This approach lets packets with SFC instructions travel across an MPLS network while following the same forwarding rules as other MPLS traffic, such as Ethernet pseudowires or VPN labels.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a brand new way to move packets with service instructions, this just uses MPLS (a method already used for lots of traffic) and adds a special label that says 'service instructions inside'.

sections.title: Label Stack Structure and Construction
sections.content:
When a Service Function Forwarder (SFF) sends an SFC packet with an NSH across an MPLS network, the sending node builds a label stack in three layers:

First, it may push zero or more labels that the destination node needs to see (such as a GAL for OAM operations). Second, it pushes the SFF Label with a Time To Live (TTL) value of 1. The TTL is set to 1 specifically to prevent mis-forwarding if the label somehow arrives at the wrong place. Third, it pushes additional labels that route the packet through the MPLS network to the destination node.

When the packet arrives at the destination MPLS node, the SFF Label will be at or near the top of the label stack. The receiving node looks up the SFF Label to find out which service function should receive the packet, then pops all the MPLS labels so that the SFF receives the packet with the NSH at the top.
sections.eli5: Building the envelope has three steps: first add any special labels for the destination, then add the big label that says 'service instructions', then add the address labels that say where the packet is going. When it arrives, remove all the MPLS labels and hand the packet with its instructions to the service.

sections.title: Processing at the Destination
sections.content:
When a packet arrives at a destination MPLS node with an SFF Label at the top, the node performs a lookup on that label to retrieve context information about the next hop. This context tells the node how to deliver the packet to the service function, such as the destination MAC address if the service function is reached over Ethernet.

The receiving SFF should check that the SFF Label has a TTL of 1 upon arrival. Any other TTL value indicates an error condition and the packet should be discarded. After the TTL check, the receiving node pops the SFF Label and any labels beneath it, leaving the NSH at the top of the packet for the service function to process.
sections.eli5: When the packet arrives, check that the label tag says it came the right way. If it did, open the envelope, remove all the MPLS wrapping, and hand the packet with its service instructions to the waiting service.

sections.title: ECMP and Load Balancing
sections.content:
MPLS routers sometimes try to balance traffic across equal-cost paths by examining the packet payload. Routers that see the first four bits of a payload as 0x4 or 0x6 might assume it is IPv4 or IPv6 and use IP header information for load balancing. The NSH Base Header was deliberately designed so that its first nibble never matches these patterns.

By default, SFC packets in an MPLS network do not use Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) load balancing based on the NSH or packet payload. All packets going to the same service function take the same path regardless of ECMP settings in the network. If ECMP load balancing is desired, two options exist: entropy labels (which add randomness to the label stack) or flow-aware transport labels. The choice between these options is left for future work.
sections.eli5: MPLS routers normally use packet headers to spread traffic across multiple paths. The NSH was designed to look unlike IP packets so routers would not try to look inside the packet. If you want to split traffic anyway, you can add special entropy labels.

sections.title: Security and OAM
sections.content:
This document follows well-established MPLS procedures and does not define any new protocol elements or code points. To the MPLS network, the NSH and its contents are opaque -- just a payload like any other. The security is no better or worse than carrying any other protocol over MPLS.

Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) at the SFC layer is handled by SFC-defined mechanisms. OAM at the MPLS transport layer can use standard MPLS OAM methods such as the Generic Associated Channel (GAL), which can be placed in the label stack below the SFF Label.
sections.eli5: This is as secure as carrying anything else over MPLS. The MPLS network does not look inside the packet, so the service chain instructions stay hidden. If you need to debug or monitor the MPLS part, standard MPLS tools work.
